conventions: Fusion status in this chapter: a contiguous group of morphemes the ASV renders by one English word is recorded `aligned` under rule 30 — עַל־כֵּן → *Wherefore* (19.7), כַּאֲשֶׁר → *as* (19.8, 19.19), לִפְנֵי → *before* (19.17 twice), מִשָּׁם → *thence* (19.12), שָׁמָּה → *thither* (19.3, 19.4), כָּל־הַיָּמִים → *ever* (19.9), בִּבְלִי־דַעַת → *unawares* (19.4), כַּזֶּה → *such* (19.20). `noncompositional` is reserved for a multi-word English rendering whose pieces cannot be assigned to particular morphemes, which in this chapter is only מִתְּמֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם → *in time past*. This is a chapter choice and not a rule: the corpus records לִפְנֵי → *before* as `aligned` in 365 units and `noncompositional` in 263, and כַּאֲשֶׁר → *as* as `aligned` in 197 and `noncompositional` in 107.

מִתְּמֹל שִׁלְשֹׁם → *in time past* is one `noncompositional` unit of all three morphemes in both DEU.19.4 and DEU.19.6, with the source head on the מִן as rule 6's deterministic anchor and the target head on the lexical noun *time*. The English expresses the idiom jointly and no morpheme owns a part of it, so rule 30's one-English-word condition is unmet and rule 2 does not split it either.

A preposition standing before תָּוֶךְ or קֶרֶב is split from it throughout this chapter, because the ASV writes a word for each morpheme every time it occurs: בְּתוֹךְ → *in* + *the midst* (19.2), בְּקֶרֶב → *in* + *the midst* (19.10, 19.20), מִקֶּרֶב → *from* + *the midst* (19.19). Rule 30's one-rendering condition is unmet in all four, so rule 2 splits them and the construct noun takes a supplied *the* under rule 29. The corpus's 27 fused preposition + תּוֹךְ/קֶרֶב → *among* units are the other shape of the same fork and do not reach a rendering the ASV writes in two words.

Where a single English *that* stands between a waw and a purpose לְ + infinitive construct, this chapter gives it to the preposition under rule 52 and leaves the waw `unrepresented`: DEU.19.3 וְהָיָה לָנוּס שָׁמָּה → *that every manslayer may flee thither* puts *that* on the לְ of לָנוּס, and both the waw and הָיָה, for which the ASV writes nothing at all, are `unrepresented`. The reasoning is that the purpose the *that* states is what לָנוּס contributes and not what the consecutive waw does. Where no infinitive stands in the clause the waw takes the *that* as usual, as at DEU.19.12 וָמֵת → *that he may die* and DEU.19.13 וְטוֹב לָךְ → *that it may go well with thee*. Rule 45 is not the competing reading here, because the ASV writes no presentative frame for הָיָה anywhere in the verse.

In the manslaughter law's אֲשֶׁר clauses, read what the ASV made of the relative before placing a supplied noun. At DEU.19.4 the clause stands in a nominal slot and the ASV writes one word for antecedent and relative together, so אֲשֶׁר takes *whoso* under rules 30 and 46. At DEU.19.5 the ASV recasts the clause adverbially as *as when a man goeth*, rendering אֲשֶׁר by the subordinator *when* and writing a lexical subject *a man* for which the Hebrew has no nominal, so that noun is its own `added` unit under rule 17. Rule 46's rider, which joins a supplied antecedent to a present relative, reaches only a clause standing in a nominal slot and only the pronoun antecedent of *him that* or *they that*. DEU.19.14's *they of old time* is neither case: רִאשֹׁנִים is written, and the whole supplied noun phrase is its rendering under rule 46.
report: Read the 46-lemma candidate table and then the full verse dump end to end, since the table is keyed by source lemma and cannot see `added` units. No cross-verse split found: every candidate group resolves to the ASV rendering one morpheme differently in different contexts, with the source or the English licensing the difference.

Checked and found uniform: preposition + TAWEK/QEREB split in all four places (19.2, 19.10, 19.19, 19.20); rule 29 article placement in every construct chain carrying a written article (19.4, 19.6, 19.12, 19.13), a present article always taking the written *the* before a supplied one, with fronting only where the rectum is rendered anarthrously, including the two-level chain of 19.12; demonstrative phrases (19.5, 19.9 twice, 19.11, 19.17, 19.20), the single written determiner going to the demonstrative with both articles unrepresented, 19.20 differing only because the ASV writes a second determiner *any*, which rule 41 gives to the article standing before the word it determines.

Also uniform: the dative LE + suffix, unrepresented before a bare English object (19.1, 19.2, 19.3, 19.8, 19.10, 19.14) and aligned wherever the ASV writes *for* (19.2, 19.7, 19.9); the apodosis waw, *then* in 19.9, 19.12, 19.17, 19.19, the rule 55 pair *and so* / *so that* in 19.5, 19.10, 19.11, and a bare *that* in 19.12, 19.13. HAYAH varies by what the ASV writes (unrepresented 19.3 and 19.11, *be* 19.10, *shall be* 19.17), and each difference is licensed by the English.

The four `added` units, which the lemma table cannot show, were read from the dump and each holds: *a man* (19.5), *if* and *and* (19.18), *shall go* (19.21). The near-miss is 19.14's *they of old time*, correctly not added, because RISHONIM is written and rule 46 gives it the noun phrase the ASV supplies to make it substantival, whereas 19.5 has no source nominal at all for *a man*.

BSB: no genuine error. The R x 14 and Td x 9 blocks are the documented convention differences (rules 27, 40, 41, 47), as are the object marker at 19.12 (rule 16) and the resumptive suffix at 19.17, which follows the contract's own ASHER BO MUM example verbatim (rules 22, 43). The one substantive case is 19.3, where BSB represents both the waw and HAYAH: the ASV writes a single *that* there, the verse pass gave it to the LE of LANUS under rule 52, and I agree, since the purpose is what the infinitive phrase contributes and not what the consecutive waw does. It is a judgment, so it is now in the log.

No promotions. The two candidates I weighed both fail the bar: the waw-versus-LE competition for a single complementizer is decided on one verse with no corpus evidence isolating that configuration, and a qualification to rule 46's rider would restate what rule 46's own 'clause with no antecedent of its own' and rule 17's supplied-subject sentence already say. Five conventions instead, including the fusion-status choice, which the corpus itself splits (LIPNE -> *before* is aligned in 365 units and noncompositional in 263) and which therefore cannot carry a rule.
